title: Being connected increasingly means mobile-only participation with narrower functional access
source_unit: Purdue Center for Regional Development Research & Policy Insights publication 124, using Census tract-level ACS and broadband-quality data
geography: United States; Census tracts in the contiguous United States

definition.value: average of households with cellular data access only and households with mobile devices only
definition.unit: composite measure; components are not mutually exclusive

observations.method: Spatial error models and Local Moran's I cluster analysis across 71,500 Census tracts in 2019 and 82,551 in 2024.
observations.uncertainty: The two snapshots are not a panel, tract geographies were not harmonized after the decennial census, and the composite measure does not count only households experiencing both constraints.
observations.subgroup: Households and places with mobile-only connectivity, limited devices, constrained data plans, disability, lower income, lower educational attainment, blue-collar employment, or weak fixed broadband.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mobile access can provide meaningful connection and may be the least-cost option; the measure shows constrained functionality and spatial association, not that mobile-only households are uniformly disconnected or harmed.

observations.method: Publication synthesis of 5-Year ACS internet-access and device-ownership measures.
observations.uncertainty: These are population-level trend measures and do not show what tasks households can complete, service quality at a particular address, or the reasons for device and plan choices.
observations.subgroup: US households moving from no internet toward cellular-data-only and mobile-device-only access.
observations.counterinterpretation: The fall in no-internet access is real progress; the report's point is that access has become more graded and functionally unequal, not that connectivity has failed.

strengthened_positive_associations.value: disability, household no-internet share, and income-related disadvantage became more strongly associated with mobile dependence
strengthened_positive_associations.unit: direction and relative strength of tract-level association

location_shift.value: metropolitan status became significantly negatively associated with mobile dependence in 2024, while age 65-plus lost significance

quality_association.value: higher fixed-broadband quality remained negatively associated with mobile dependence, but the association weakened

observations.method: Spatial error regression using tract socioeconomic, demographic, housing, employment, internet-access, and fixed-broadband-quality variables.
observations.uncertainty: Associations are ecological and cannot establish that disability, income, broadband quality, or pandemic-era changes caused a household's mobile dependence.
observations.subgroup: Census tracts differentiated by disability, income, education, housing tenure, age, race/ethnicity, employment type, metropolitan status, and broadband quality.
observations.counterinterpretation: The changing associations may reflect migration, changed tract composition, measurement shifts, or the interaction of affordability and infrastructure rather than one single mechanism.

deployment_limit.value: infrastructure deployment alone may be insufficient when the resulting connection remains mobile-only

next_layer.value: affordability, devices, digital literacy, accessibility, and housing wiring need to accompany network buildout

service_risk.value: essential services moving online can impose higher functional costs on small-screen, capped-data households

observations.method: Author interpretation of the measured mobile-dependence trend, spatial associations, and broadband-policy context.
observations.uncertainty: The publication does not measure service outcomes, task completion, affordability changes, or causal effects of BEAD, ACP expiration, or digital-literacy programs.
observations.subgroup: Households expected to use digital public services, education, work, health, commerce, and civic systems through constrained mobile pathways.
observations.counterinterpretation: Mobile plans and smartphones may be adaptive, convenient, and adequate for many tasks; the policy implication concerns option breadth and resilience, not a universal hierarchy of devices.

boundary: This record adds a US structural digital-participation trend: fewer households are offline, but more rely on mobile-only access with narrower device and data capacity. It does not establish individual household causality, service failure, digital-harm prevalence, or the effects of any broadband or subsidy program.
